newsitem.title: BELGIUM: A dozen countries now lobby for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: A dozen countries now lobby for NATO membership.

text.p: A total of 12 former communist countries in central and eastern Europe want to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), which was created in 1949 to defend the West from attack by the Soviet Union.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, desperate to join the Euro-Atlantic democratic institutions which Stalinism denied them at the end of World War Two, lead the field, but Slovenia and Romania are pushing hard too.
The first three countries have met the main conditions of establishing market economies, respect of human rights, and democratic control of the armed forces since the Soviet bloc broke up.

Working closer with NATO under its Partnership for Peace programme and alongside Western countries in the multinational peace force in Bosnia, they have also made enormous progress bringing their armed forces in line with alliance standards.

Crucially, all three are also supported by vocal and influential lobbies in the United States, by far the alliance's most important member and the country most keen on completing the expansion by NATO's 50th anniversary in two years time.

All applicants are also clamouring to join the European Union, a more complicated process which could take several more years to achieve -- the growing awareness of which has pushed NATO enlargement to the forefront of the international agenda.
Romania, strongly backed by France which has close historical ties, has suddenly emerged as the most likely outsider to make the first wave.
Supporters say the country, which has won praise for widescale military reforms, should be rewarded for recently completing its long transition from hardline communism to democracy without bloodshed.
Critics say its impoverished economy simply would not allow it to carry the burden implied by membership of the most powerful military alliance ever assembled.
Tiny Slovenia, which escaped the worst of the wars accompanying the break up of former Yugoslavia, is also frequently cited as a country which may make it at the first attempt.
It fulfils all the main conditions and now boasts a successful and growing economy. NATO's military favour its inclusion because it would give a vital landlink from NATO member Italy to Hungary.
Politicians say membership would also show Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia the likely benefits in store if peace and democracy take root in the Balkans.

Against that, however, is the strong argument that NATO, which works on the basis of consensus among its 16 members, could not absorb more than three countries at this stage and still survive as a credible organisation.
Membership for the Baltic States of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia is currently ruled out as simply too risky whatever arguments in favour are advanced.
Moscow, which relucantly may accept a limited enlargement to include former Warsaw Pact countries, would draw the line at former Soviet republic joining its Cold War foes.

Instead, the United States is pushing the European allies to treat the countries separately, rather than as a bloc, and to try to deepen links with the 15-nation European Union as a sort of "soft security guarantee".

Bulgaria, which until recently said it did not want membership, now has changed its mind, but is too far behind to have any realistic chance in this round. Albania and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia have also applied, but are currently rooted firmly at the bottom of the pack.
